epithet: Hibb Rasulillah (the Beloved of the Messenger of Allah)
tribe: Banu Kalb (maternal) / freed clients of Quraysh
role: Commander of the last army dispatched by the Prophet ﷺ
Son of Zayd ibn Harithah, the adopted son of the Prophet ﷺ
summary: Usamah ibn Zayd (RA) was the son of Zayd ibn Harithah and Umm Ayman, raised in the household of the Prophet ﷺ from infancy. Beloved by the Prophet ﷺ, he was appointed commander of the final expedition the Prophet ﷺ organised before his death, at around seventeen or eighteen years of age — a command that drew objections which the Prophet ﷺ firmly rejected.
biography:
Usamah ibn Zayd ibn Harithah al-Kalbi was born around 614 CE in Makkah. His father, Zayd ibn Harithah, had been enslaved as a child, then purchased and freed by the Prophet ﷺ, who loved him as a son — Zayd was at one point called 'Zayd ibn Muhammad' before the Quran abrogated the practice of adoptive filiation. His mother, Umm Ayman (Barakah al-Habashiyyah), had been the nursemaid of the Prophet ﷺ since childhood and was treated by him with the deepest respect and affection. Usamah thus grew up in the Prophet's household, and the Prophet ﷺ loved him intensely from his earliest childhood.

The Prophet ﷺ used to carry Usamah on one knee and Hasan ibn Ali on the other, holding both boys close and saying: 'O Allah, have mercy on them, for I have mercy on them.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Adab). He called Usamah 'our beloved son of our beloved,' and the Sahaba called him 'Hibb Rasulillah' — the Beloved of Allah's Messenger. Al-Dhahabi records in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' that when Usamah walked, the Prophet ﷺ would watch him with visible delight.

Usamah fought in several expeditions from a young age. He attempted to join the Battle of Uhud in 3 AH but was turned away by the Prophet ﷺ as too young, at around eight or nine years old. He was permitted to fight in the Battle of al-Khandaq (the Trench, 5 AH) and subsequent campaigns. Ibn Sa'd records in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra that Usamah participated in the campaign to Mu'tah in 8 AH, where his father Zayd was killed as the first commander.

In 11 AH (632 CE), in the final weeks of his life, the Prophet ﷺ organised a large expedition to the region of Ubna near the Syrian border — in part to avenge the losses at Mu'tah and to reassert Muslim presence on the northern frontier. He appointed Usamah ibn Zayd as its commander, at an age variously reported between seventeen and twenty years old. This appointment provoked open murmuring among some of the older Sahaba and Ansar, who questioned whether a youth of such age was fit to command veterans. The Prophet ﷺ responded with unmistakable firmness. He rose in the mosque, addressed the community, praised Usamah and his father, and declared: 'If you are criticising Usamah's appointment as commander, you were similarly critical of his father's appointment before him. By Allah, he was fit for command, and this son of his is fit for command after him.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Maghazi). The Prophet ﷺ did not relent from this appointment despite his illness intensifying.

The Prophet ﷺ died before the army of Usamah departed. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, upon becoming Caliph, insisted the army proceed despite the ridda uprisings breaking out across Arabia, saying: 'I will not untie a flag that the Prophet of Allah tied.' Usamah led the expedition, which was conducted successfully, and returned to Madinah after the ridda situation stabilised.

Usamah lived through the caliphates of Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, and Ali (RA). He withdrew from active military or political involvement during the period of civil strife (fitnah) between Ali and Muawiyah, stating his famous position that he would not fight a man who said 'La ilaha illa Allah.' Al-Dhahabi records that he lived in Wadi al-Qura near Madinah and died there around 54 AH (674 CE), though some sources give 58 AH. He is counted among the senior narrators of hadith, and his reports are found in all six major collections. The Prophet's tender love for him remained one of the most frequently cited examples of his personal warmth toward children of those close to him.

Principled withdrawal from civil strife — refused to fight any Muslim who professed the shahada
Known for loyalty and quietude rather than political ambition
